overview: Diplodocus carnegii ("Carnegie's double beam") was one of the longest animals ever to walk the Earth, reaching 26 metres, though far lighter than the stocky Brachiosaurus at around 15 tonnes. Its neck was held roughly horizontally rather than upright, and the peg-like teeth at the very front of the snout were used exclusively for raking leaves from branches — Diplodocus could not chew and processed no food in the mouth at all.

Andrew Carnegie funded plaster casts of the famous specimen "Dippy" that were shipped to eight museums across Europe, making Diplodocus the most publicly recognised sauropod of the 20th century. The NHM London's Dippy stood in the main entrance hall for 112 years before being replaced by the blue whale skeleton Hope in 2017.

articles.title: Carnegie and the plaster Dippies
articles.body: Andrew Carnegie funded expeditions that recovered the CM 84 specimen from Wyoming in 1899. After seeing a newspaper illustration, Carnegie commissioned eight full-scale plaster casts for European royalty — gifts to the natural history museums of London, Paris, Berlin, Vienna, Bologna, La Plata, Saint Petersburg and Madrid. This act of scientific philanthropy made Diplodocus the most-recognised dinosaur skeleton in the world for much of the 20th century.

articles.title: Feeding mechanism
articles.body: The pencil-like peg teeth of Diplodocus are positioned only at the front of the snout and show heavy wear on their tips — consistent with raking leaves off branches. No shearing or grinding occurs in the mouth; food was swallowed whole and processed by gastroliths (stomach stones) and fermentation. This feeding strategy allowed Diplodocus to strip enormous volumes of vegetation rapidly, an efficient if crude approach for a 15-tonne browser.

articles.title: Neck posture debate
articles.body: Computer modelling of Diplodocus neck vertebrae and joint mobility consistently suggests the neck was held near-horizontal or at a slight upward angle — very different from the giraffe-like posture of early reconstructions. At maximum horizontal extension the neck allowed feeding across a wide swathe of ground-level vegetation without moving the body, an efficient strategy for a very large animal whose locomotion was energetically costly.

record.description: Diplodocus was a long-necked diplodocid sauropod from the Morrison Formation of western North America. D. carnegii and related material provide several substantial skeletons and skulls, but famous museum mounts are composites and species assignments have been extensively revised.
facts: The Carnegie mount combines principal specimens and reconstructed parts; it is not one complete individual.
Peg-like front teeth and low skull support selective cropping, while exact vegetation and feeding height varied with posture.
Extreme tail-whip speeds and supersonic cracking remain biomechanical hypotheses rather than consensus facts.

review.ageReviewNote: Most diagnostic Diplodocus material comes from Kimmeridgian-Tithonian Morrison intervals near 154-152 Ma.
